newsitem.title: USA: Corn, soybeans firm on weather, oil falls.
newsitem.headline: Corn, soybeans firm on weather, oil falls.

text.p: Corn and soybean prices rose on Wednesday as weather forecasters predicted that rains expected this weekend in the Midwest would remain north of many parched fields in the region.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans for post-harvest delivery in November rose 15-1/2 cents a bushel to close at $6.50. December corn closed 4-1/4 cents higher at $2.61-1/2.

"You change the weather forecast, you change the market," said Dale Durchholz, analyst with Agrivisor Services. "The whole soybean market is directly correlated to the weather right now. Any little subtle tweak in the forecast is going to move prices."
Weather Services Corp senior agricultural meteorologist David Taylor said showers may be lightest in the areas where corn and soybean crops most need moisture.
"Right now it looks like we will have the hardest time getting decent rain in the Illinois and Indiana area," he said.

The Massachusetts-based weather agency predicted a weekend storm system would bring one-quarter to one inch of rain to the U.S. Corn Belt on Sunday or Monday with 40 to 60 percent coverage of the region.
That scenario differed from some wetter outlooks issued earlier this week that contributed to sharp drops in soybeans.

"The only thing in here today was the dry weather. Weather Services never has been wet, they were dry Monday and they're still dry which is what I'm banking on," said Tom Levis, analyst for Prudential Securities.
Corn and soybeans are both now in a crucial period of growth when corn kermels and soybean pods are being shaped and filled. Moisture and lack of heat stress are keys to yields.
Wheat prices also finished strong on ideas that exports were picking up. December wheat closed 8-3/4 cents a bushel higher at $3.77.
"There's talk about a lot of exports coming in but I haven't seen it, just bits and pieces here and there. But the Egyptian business may come in," said Levis.
There was talk that Egypt may call a snap tender to buy 200,000 to 300,000 tons of U.S. wheat as early as the weekend, which would complete Egypt's September requirements.
Morocco said it would seek 90,000 tons of wheat next week, Pakistan may re-enter the market soon and European traders said Iraq had bought 50,000 metric tons of U.S. hard wheat.

The Iraqi purchase was tied to its imminent resumption of oil sales under a United Nations plan to allow Iraq to sell up to $2.14 billion of oil over six months to raise funds to buy food, medicines and other humanitarian supplies.
Those Iraqi oil sales, originally slated to start from June 8, have been held up as the U.N. approved Iraq's plan to distribute the goods.
The U.N. has imposed trade sanctions on Iraq since its troops invaded Kuwait in August 1990, triggering the Gulf War.

Those potential Iraqi supplies have been hanging over the crude oil market for weeks. So when Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Muhammed Rasheed said in Baghdad on Wednesday that the sales would commernce in mid-August, oil prices fell.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil for September delivery fell 35 cents a barrel to close at $20.46.

"The traders who were long gasoline were finally throwing in the towel as Iraqi oil sales became the main news feature which also overwhelmed Cano Limon's problems," said Todd Miller, an oil trader with Morgan Stanley in New York.

Occidental Corp shut down its Cano Limon field in Colombia earlier this week after landslides and attacks by guerrillas damaged a pipeline carrying the field's crude oil to port terminals. The field produces about 175,000 barrels of oil a day.
September gasoline settled 1.04 cent a gallon lower at 66.06 cents and September heating oil ended 1.34 cents a gallon lower at 56.98 cents.
